title: Cell biology
summary: The structure, transport, signalling and life cycle of cells.

layers.basics: The cell is the smallest unit of life. Cells have membranes, organelles, a skeleton, ways to move materials, ways to talk to each other and a cycle of growth and division.
layers.deeper: Prokaryotic cells are simple and small; eukaryotic cells have a nucleus and compartments. Compartments let a cell run incompatible chemistry side by side and target proteins to the right place.
layers.expert: Cell behaviour emerges from networks: signalling pathways convert external cues to gene-expression and cytoskeletal changes, while checkpoints tie growth to division and trigger apoptosis when damage is irreparable.

title: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

layers.basics: Prokaryotes (bacteria and archaea) lack a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. Eukaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleus and have compartments.
layers.deeper: Prokaryotes are typically 0.5–5 µm and eukaryotes 10–100 µm. Both have ribosomes, DNA and a plasma membrane.
layers.expert: Eukaryotes arose from an archaeal host that acquired a bacterial endosymbiont. Eukaryotic cell volume is ≈ 1,000–10,000× that of a bacterium. One influential hypothesis is that mitochondria supplied the energy per gene needed to support large genomes; later analyses question how large that energy gap really is, so the idea is debated.

open_questions: Which archaeal lineage was the host, why complex cells arose only once, and whether mitochondrial energy made large genomes possible are still debated.

title: Cell size and surface-area-to-volume ratio

layers.basics: As a cell grows, volume increases faster than surface area, so it becomes harder to supply and clear the interior.
layers.deeper: This is why cells divide, why gut lining and lung surfaces are folded, and why large cells use many small compartments.
layers.expert: For a sphere SA/V = 3/r. Diffusion time scales with distance squared (t ≈ x²/2D in one dimension). In water, where a small molecule has D ≈ 10⁻⁹ m²/s, it covers 10 µm in about 50 ms but 1 mm in about 8 minutes. Cytoplasm is more crowded, so small molecules diffuse several times more slowly there and the times are correspondingly longer.

facts: ≈ 50 ms in water (several times longer in cytoplasm)
formula: t ≈ x²/(2D) in one dimension (x²/(6D) in three)

title: Fluid mosaic membrane
summary: Proteins floating in a lipid bilayer.

layers.basics: The plasma membrane is a fluid bilayer of phospholipids with proteins, cholesterol and carbohydrates embedded.
layers.deeper: Lipids and many proteins move sideways; cholesterol buffers fluidity. Membrane proteins act as channels, pumps, receptors and anchors.
layers.expert: Cytoskeletal fences confine many membrane proteins into domains, and the membrane is asymmetric between leaflets. Membrane composition changes with temperature (homeoviscous adaptation). Whether lipid rafts, small ordered lipid patches, exist as stable domains in living cells is still debated.

facts: ≈ 50% in a typical plasma membrane (about 18–75% across membranes)
open_questions: Whether lipid rafts exist as stable ordered domains in living cells, and how large and long-lived they are, is debated.

title: Diffusion and osmosis

layers.basics: Particles spread from high to low concentration (diffusion). Water follows by osmosis across a semipermeable membrane toward higher solute concentration.
layers.deeper: Small nonpolar molecules (O2, CO2) cross membranes directly. Cells in hypotonic solution swell, in hypertonic solution shrink; plant walls prevent bursting.
layers.expert: Fick's first law gives flux J = −D dC/dx. Expressing the aquaporin CHIP28 (AQP1) in Xenopus oocytes raised their osmotic water permeability (Preston et al., 1992); Peter Agre received the 2003 Nobel for their discovery.

facts: Diffusion coefficient of glucose in water
≈ 3×10⁹ water molecules/s per channel (AQP1 monomer; an estimate)

title: Channels and carriers (facilitated diffusion)
summary: Proteins that help specific molecules cross.

layers.basics: Channel and carrier proteins let ions and polar molecules cross membranes without energy, always downhill.
layers.deeper: Ion channels can be gated by voltage, ligand or force. GLUT transporters move glucose into cells.
layers.expert: Channels pass up to about 10⁷–10⁸ ions per second, while carriers cycle at about 10²–10⁴ per second. The selectivity filter of a K⁺ channel replaces the ion's water shell with oxygen atoms from the protein backbone; exactly why this excludes Na⁺ is still studied.

facts: at least ≈ 1000:1 over Na⁺ (varies by channel)

title: Active transport and the Na⁺/K⁺ pump

layers.basics: The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to push 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in. It builds and maintains the ion gradients.
layers.deeper: It uses a large share of resting ATP, and the share depends on cell type and conditions; one review puts it at over 80% of ATP turnover in neurons. Secondary active transport (e.g. SGLT) uses the sodium gradient to import glucose.
layers.expert: P-type ATPases phosphorylate an aspartate in the cycle. Digoxin inhibits the pump and raises intracellular Ca²⁺ in the heart. Co-transport and antiport couple solute movement to ion gradients.

facts: 3 Na⁺ out : 2 K⁺ in per ATP
Share of ATP used by the pump

layers.basics: Cells engulf material by endocytosis and release it by exocytosis, using membrane vesicles.
layers.deeper: Types include phagocytosis (cell eating), pinocytosis (cell drinking) and receptor-mediated endocytosis, which captures cholesterol-carrying LDL.
layers.expert: Clathrin coats and dynamin pinch off vesicles; SNARE proteins mediate vesicle fusion. Defective LDL receptor endocytosis causes familial hypercholesterolemia.

layers.basics: Cells are electrically polarised, with the inside negative. Ion gradients and selective channels create this resting voltage.
layers.deeper: Resting potential is ≈ −70 mV in neurons, set mainly by K+ leak channels. Changes in this voltage are the basis of nerve signals.
layers.expert: The Goldman–Hodgkin–Katz equation weights each ion by permeability. Mitochondria keep the matrix roughly 150–180 mV negative of the intermembrane space, depending on cell state.

layers.basics: The nucleus holds chromosomes inside a double membrane with pores. The nucleolus inside builds ribosome parts.
layers.deeper: Nuclear pore complexes regulate traffic between nucleus and cytoplasm; mRNA exits while transcription factors enter.
layers.expert: A vertebrate pore is ≈ 110–125 MDa (a yeast pore is about half that) and is built from about 30 different nucleoporins; one pore can handle on the order of 10³ translocations per second (an estimate). The lamina gives mechanical support; mutations in lamin A cause progeria.

title: Secretory pathway and protein targeting
summary: Getting proteins to the right place.

layers.basics: Proteins destined for secretion or membranes are made on ER-bound ribosomes, folded and glycosylated in the ER, sorted in the Golgi, and shipped in vesicles.
layers.deeper: A short signal sequence on the new chain directs most ER proteins to the ER. Other signals send proteins to the nucleus and mitochondria, and lysosomal enzymes are tagged with mannose-6-phosphate in the Golgi.
layers.expert: The signal recognition particle (SRP) pauses translation and docks the ribosome onto the translocon (Sec61). Mannose-6-phosphate tags direct enzymes to lysosomes; I-cell disease results from loss of the tagging enzyme.

title: Autophagy

layers.basics: In autophagy a membrane wraps cytoplasm or damaged organelles and delivers them to lysosomes for breakdown and recycling.
layers.deeper: It is activated by starvation and stress, and clears damaged mitochondria (mitophagy) and aggregates. Yoshinori Ohsumi won the 2016 Nobel for discovering its mechanisms.
layers.expert: The ATG gene family drives phagophore formation; mTOR inhibition triggers it. Impaired autophagy is linked to neurodegeneration and cancer, but tumours can also exploit it, so the effect of boosting or blocking it depends on context.

open_questions: Whether boosting or blocking autophagy helps in cancer and neurodegeneration depends on context and is not settled.

title: Endosymbiotic theory

layers.basics: Mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from free-living bacteria that came to live inside ancestral cells. They keep a small genome and their own ribosomes and divide by fission, but most of the proteins they need are made from nuclear genes.
layers.deeper: Evidence: circular DNA, bacterial-type ribosomes, double membranes, and genes that most closely resemble those of alpha-proteobacteria (the exact bacterial relative of mitochondria is debated) and cyanobacteria (chloroplasts). Lynn Margulis championed the idea in 1967.
layers.expert: Most endosymbiont genes have moved to the nucleus; the human mtDNA retains only 37 genes (16.6 kb). Secondary endosymbiosis explains algae with 3–4 membranes around plastids. The identity of the archaeal host (Asgard archaea) is still being tested.

open_questions: Asgard archaea are the closest known relatives of the host, but how the first endosymbiont entered, how complex the host already was, and when mitochondria were acquired relative to eukaryotic complexity (early or late) are still debated.

title: Chloroplasts and plastids
summary: Plant organelles for photosynthesis and storage.

layers.basics: Chloroplasts hold stacks of thylakoid membranes (grana) where light reactions occur, in a fluid called stroma.
layers.deeper: Other plastids store starch (amyloplasts) or pigments (chromoplasts). Chloroplast numbers per leaf cell range from ≈ 20 to 100.
layers.expert: Chloroplast genomes are ≈ 120–160 kb with ≈ 100–130 genes. Chloroplasts import ≈ 3,000 proteins using TOC/TIC translocons.

title: Cell walls and extracellular matrix
summary: Outer layers that support and connect cells.

layers.basics: Plant cells have cellulose walls, most bacteria have peptidoglycan walls and fungi have walls of chitin and glucan. Animal cells are embedded in an extracellular matrix of collagen and other proteins.
layers.deeper: Walls resist osmotic bursting; the ECM carries signals and guides cell migration. Collagen is the most abundant protein in the human body.
layers.expert: Integrins link the ECM to the actin cytoskeleton and transmit mechanical signals (mechanotransduction). Primary vs secondary plant walls differ in composition; lignin makes wood rigid.

title: Cell junctions
summary: How neighbouring cells attach and communicate.

layers.basics: Tight junctions seal gaps between cells, desmosomes act as spot rivets, and gap junctions form channels that let small molecules pass.
layers.deeper: Plant cells connect through plasmodesmata. Junctions let tissues act as units, for example synchronising heart cells.
layers.expert: Vertebrate gap junctions are made of connexins (invertebrates use innexins) and pass molecules up to roughly 1 kDa. Tight junctions (claudins, occludin) set epithelial barrier properties and the blood–brain barrier.

facts: ≈ 30 nm wide and ≈ 100 nm long (simple type); only the narrow cytoplasmic sleeve is open to traffic

title: Microtubules and motor proteins
summary: Tracks and trucks inside the cell.

layers.basics: Microtubules are hollow tubes of tubulin that form tracks. Kinesin and dynein motors walk along them carrying cargo.
layers.deeper: Microtubules form the mitotic spindle and the core of cilia and flagella. Kinesin steps ≈ 8 nm per ATP.
layers.expert: Dynamic instability (growth and catastrophe) lets spindles search and capture chromosomes. Taxol stabilises microtubules and kills dividing cells, and colchicine prevents polymerisation.

layers.basics: Actin filaments drive crawling, pinch cells in two and work with myosin in muscle. Intermediate filaments such as keratin give tensile strength.
layers.deeper: Actin polymerises at one end and shrinks at the other (treadmilling), pushing the leading edge of moving cells.
layers.expert: Arp2/3 nucleates branched actin networks; formins nucleate straight filaments. Intermediate filament types are tissue-specific and used as diagnostic markers.

title: Cell signaling: ligands, receptors and responses
summary: How cells sense and answer messages.

layers.basics: A signalling molecule (ligand) binds a receptor, which starts a chain of events inside the cell leading to a response.
layers.deeper: Signals can act at a distance (endocrine), nearby (paracrine), on themselves (autocrine) or by direct contact. Receptors are at the surface or inside.
layers.expert: Signalling networks add amplification, feedback and crosstalk. Response specificity arises from receptor type, scaffold proteins and cell context; receptor affinities (K_d) span roughly picomolar to micromolar, and many hormone receptors bind in the nanomolar range or tighter.

facts: K_d ≈ pM–µM; often nM for hormone receptors

layers.basics: A GPCR spans the membrane seven times. When a ligand binds, it activates a G protein that triggers second messengers.
layers.deeper: About a third of approved drugs act on GPCRs, including beta blockers and antihistamines. Vision, smell and adrenaline responses use them.
layers.expert: Gα exchanges GDP for GTP and dissociates from Gβγ; Gs activates adenylyl cyclase (cAMP), Gq activates PLC (IP3/DAG). β-arrestin terminates and redirects signalling. Lefkowitz and Kobilka won the 2012 Nobel.

title: Receptor tyrosine kinases and kinase cascades

layers.basics: When a growth factor binds an RTK, receptors pair up and phosphorylate each other. This starts cascades such as Ras–MAP kinase.
layers.deeper: Cascades amplify the signal and end in changes to transcription factors. Mutations that lock Ras or RTKs "on" drive many cancers.
layers.expert: SH2 domains dock to phosphotyrosines, Grb2/SOS activates Ras, and the Raf–MEK–ERK module relays the signal. Kinase inhibitors act on such signalling: gefitinib blocks the receptor EGFR, and imatinib blocks the kinases BCR-ABL, KIT and PDGFR.

facts: ≈ 20–25% of human cancers (KRAS, NRAS, HRAS together)

title: Second messengers and calcium signalling
summary: Small molecules that spread the message.

layers.basics: cAMP, IP3, diacylglycerol and Ca²⁺ are small second messengers that relay and amplify signals.
layers.deeper: Cytosolic Ca²⁺ rises from ≈ 100 nM to ≈ 1 µM when channels open, triggering muscle contraction, secretion and fertilisation responses.
layers.expert: Calmodulin binds Ca²⁺ and switches on enzymes such as CaMKII, which can decode the frequency of Ca²⁺ oscillations. Phosphodiesterases degrade cAMP; caffeine inhibits them only at high, non-physiological doses, and at normal doses it mainly blocks adenosine receptors. Signal amplification: one activated receptor can generate thousands of second messengers.

title: Steroid and nuclear receptors
summary: Hormones that act directly on gene expression.

layers.basics: Steroid hormones such as cortisol and estrogen cross the membrane freely, and thyroid hormone enters through transporters; all bind receptors that act as transcription factors.
layers.deeper: The hormone–receptor complex binds hormone response elements in DNA and turns genes on or off. Effects are slower but longer lasting than membrane receptors.
layers.expert: The nuclear receptor superfamily has ≈ 48 human members. Many drugs (tamoxifen, glucocorticoids) target them.

title: The cell cycle

layers.basics: G1 is the main growth phase, DNA is copied in S, and the cell finishes preparing in G2 and divide in M phase (mitosis and cytokinesis).
layers.deeper: Cell cycle lengths vary: ≈ 24 h in typical cultured human cells, ≈ 20 min for E. coli in ideal conditions, and G0 for cells that exit the cycle such as neurons.
layers.expert: Cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) partner with cyclins, whose abundance oscillates. Three main checkpoints: G1/S, G2/M and the spindle checkpoint in metaphase.

facts: ≈ 24 h (in the body, from hours to years)

title: Cell-cycle control, checkpoints and tumour suppressors

layers.basics: Checkpoints stop the cycle if DNA is damaged or chromosomes are not aligned. Proteins like p53 and Rb act as brakes.
layers.deeper: Cyclin–CDK complexes push the cycle forward; p21 and p27 inhibit them. Mutated p53 is found in roughly a third to a half of human cancers, depending on the dataset.
layers.expert: Rb holds E2F transcription factors until phosphorylated by CDK4/6. the kinases ATM and ATR detect DNA damage and activate p53, which then induces arrest, repair or apoptosis; the anaphase-promoting complex triggers separation of sister chromatids.

facts: ≈ 35–50% of human cancers, depending on the dataset

title: Cytokinesis and binary fission

layers.basics: Animal cells pinch in two with a ring of actin and myosin; plant cells build a new wall; bacteria divide by binary fission.
layers.deeper: Bacteria use FtsZ, a tubulin relative, to form a ring at mid-cell. Under ideal conditions E. coli can divide every ≈ 20 min.
layers.expert: Cytokinesis is positioned by the spindle midzone and regulated by RhoA. Min proteins in bacteria oscillate to keep the division ring at the centre.

facts: ≈ 20 min in rich medium at 37 °C (hours in poor conditions)

title: Apoptosis and cell death

layers.basics: Apoptosis is an orderly, controlled way for cells to die. It shapes tissues in development and removes damaged cells.
layers.deeper: A cascade of caspase enzymes cuts cell components. The cell shrinks, blebs and is eaten by neighbours without causing inflammation, unlike necrosis. Cells can also die by regulated non-apoptotic routes, including necroptosis, pyroptosis and ferroptosis, which do provoke inflammation.
layers.expert: Intrinsic pathway: mitochondrial cytochrome c release and apoptosome; extrinsic: death receptors (Fas). BCL-2 family proteins balance survival. In the C. elegans hermaphrodite, 131 of the 1,090 somatic cells made during development die by programmed cell death.

facts: Adult human cells turned over per day

title: Stem cells and differentiation
summary: Cells that can renew and become specialised.

layers.basics: Stem cells divide to renew themselves and to produce cells that specialise. Embryonic stem cells are pluripotent: they can give rise to nearly every cell type of the body, but not to a whole organism with its placenta.
layers.deeper: Adult stem cells (bone marrow, gut crypts, skin) maintain tissues. Reprogramming adult cells to induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSC) won Shinya Yamanaka and John Gurdon (whose nuclear-transfer work showed that mature nuclei can be reprogrammed) the 2012 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
layers.expert: Pluripotency is maintained by OCT4, SOX2 and NANOG; differentiation involves epigenetic restriction. Applications include disease modelling, organoids and cell therapy; safety concerns include tumour formation.

title: Telomeres, senescence and ageing

layers.basics: Telomeres are repeated DNA caps at chromosome ends that shorten with each division. When short, cells stop dividing (senescence).
layers.deeper: Telomerase rebuilds telomeres in stem and germ cells and is reactivated in most cancers. Hayflick and Moorhead found that cultured human fetal fibroblasts stop after about 50 ± 10 doublings.
layers.expert: The human telomere repeat is TTAGGG; telomeres are several to about 15 kb long at birth, vary between people and cell types, and shorten with age. Senescent cells secrete inflammatory factors (SASP); clearing them extends healthspan in mice. How much telomere loss drives human ageing is still being studied.

open_questions: How much replicative senescence and telomere erosion contribute to organismal ageing versus other hallmarks is unresolved.
